clue.text: Overawed by the famous Leo and Van?

blocks.note: Leo is a constellation, a group of stars
a van is a small truck

explanation.surface: Someone is dazzled at meeting Leo DiCaprio and Van Morrison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leo' and 'Van' look like famous first names, but Leo is the constellation and the van is a vehicle. The definition swallows 'the famous' too.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone star-struck is dazzled and tongue-tied in the presence of celebrities, the very meaning of being overawed by them.

clue.text: Sibling drinking soft drinks

indicators.note: whatever drinks takes something inside itself, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: sis is short for sister
p (piano) is the musical marking for soft

explanation.surface: A brother or sister is having fizzy pop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soft drinks' reads as one phrase, but 'soft' belongs to the wordplay and 'drinks' alone is the definition, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To sip is to drink in small mouthfuls, so a verb meaning takes little drinks fits the third-person verb.

clue.text: Cracked vase and bowl – wife emerging for excuse!

indicators.note: something emerging comes out of where it was, so that letter leaves the group
cracked things are broken into pieces, so the letters are smashed and rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, minus the wife's letter
W is the abbreviation for wife; it is removed

explanation.surface: Someone who broke the crockery hopes the wife turning up will give them an excuse.
explanation.walkthrough: Take W out of VASE plus BOWL and rearrange the seven letters left.
explanation.definitionFit: To absolve someone is to free them from blame, which is what excusing a person does.

clue.text: Country tune tipped by southern Yankee

indicators.note: a thing tipped up is turned over, and in a down entry that turns the letters upside down

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for southern
Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet
an air is a tune

explanation.surface: A country-music song is beaten into second place by an American from the South.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country tune' reads as a music genre, but 'Country' is the definition. In a down clue, 'tipped by' puts the upturned piece underneath S and Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Syria is a nation in the Middle East, an example of the general class named by the definition.

clue.text: One second behind Victor, smuggler on horseback

blocks.note: a runner smuggles goods, as in gunrunner or rum-runner
a jockey who is up is riding the horse

explanation.surface: A contraband carrier rides one second behind a man called Victor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victor' looks like a name or the NATO letter V, but it means the winner; the definition is the whole opening phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The runner-up finishes in second place, just behind whoever wins a race or contest.

clue.text: Groom given ring in small group

blocks.note: to groom hair is to comb it
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: A bridegroom receives his wedding ring among a small party of friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groom' suggests a wedding, but here it is the verb for tidying hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A combo is a small band of musicians, typically playing jazz, so it names a little ensemble of players.

clue.text: Son, shy layabout

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
to shy is to throw, and so is to lob

explanation.surface: A parent describes a timid son who lounges around all day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shy' reads as timid, but it is the verb meaning to throw, as at a coconut shy.
explanation.definitionFit: A slob is a lazy, untidy person, which is what a layabout is.

clue.text: Disappointment, left in Paris and not working

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for left
et is French for and
a system that is down is not working

explanation.surface: A disappointing trip: stuck in Paris with everything out of order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Paris' is the convention for putting the next word into French.
explanation.definitionFit: A let-down is an anticlimax, something that fails to live up to hopes, which is a disappointment.

clue.text: Ready to take someone out?

blocks.note: surface reading: prepared to escort someone on a date
setter's reading: ready is slang for cash, paid for taking someone out, that is killing them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is a noun, as in 'readies', British slang for cash, and 'take out' means to assassinate.
explanation.definitionFit: Blood money is the fee paid to a hired killer, cash handed over for murdering a victim.

clue.text: Stand waving pet’s lead

indicators.note: something waving moves to and fro, so these letters are jumbled into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone stands waving their dog's lead about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand' looks like a verb but it is the noun, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedestal is the base or support on which a statue or column rests, a kind of stand.

clue.text: Hard to split from comparatively high-class model

indicators.note: to split from something is to break away and leave it, so a letter departs

blocks.note: posh means high-class; the comparative adds -er
H is the pencil-lead abbreviation for hard; it is removed

explanation.surface: A model finds it hard to break up with a richer partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard' looks like a description of the split, but it is the letter H that leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who poses for an artist or photographer is a poser, which is what a model does.

clue.text: Unfeeling, wrote off deputy

indicators.note: food that has gone off has spoiled, so these letters are spoilt into a new order

blocks.note: numb means without feeling
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A heartless boss coldly dismissed their second-in-command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrote off' reads as a phrasal verb, dismissing someone, but 'off' signals rearranging the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A number two is a second-in-command, the person who stands in for the leader, like a deputy.

clue.text: Maybe spinach with lunchtime bitter doesn’t impress

blocks.note: spinach is an example of leaves eaten as a vegetable
one o'clock is lunchtime
bitter weather is very cold

explanation.surface: Spinach served with a lunchtime pint of bitter is an underwhelming meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bitter' suggests the British beer, but it is the adjective for freezing weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that leaves one cold fails to stir any interest or enthusiasm, an idiom for failing to excite.

clue.text: Audible sound of car horn fixed, scout’s saying

indicators.note: audible means able to be heard, so the answer is judged by the ear rather than by spelling

blocks.note: a car horn's sound is a beep, and fixed means repaired

explanation.surface: A mechanic mends a car's horn as a scout recites a motto.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'beep repaired' runs together into the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Be Prepared is the motto of the Scout movement, coined by its founder Baden-Powell.

clue.text: Busy flat beginning to trouble female university student

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: a flat surface is even
the first letter of the word
F is the abbreviation for female
U is the abbreviation for university
L for learner, a student

explanation.surface: A crowded student flat is the start of trouble for a woman at university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Busy flat' reads as a noisy apartment, but 'Busy' alone is the definition. L for learner comes from the learner-driver plates.
explanation.definitionFit: An eventful day is full of happenings, so the word describes a busy period with plenty going on.

clue.text: Moving about

blocks.note: first meaning: emotionally affecting
second meaning: concerning

explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving about' reads as walking around; it is two separate meanings, an adjective and a preposition.
explanation.definitionFit: A touching story stirs the emotions, and the old preposition touching means regarding or with respect to.

clue.text: Fuss over drunk

blocks.note: to kick up a stink is to make a fuss
O is the cricket abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: Someone makes a scene about a person who has had too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' looks like a preposition linking the words, but it supplies O.
explanation.definitionFit: Stinko is a slang word for very intoxicated, a colloquial adjective for someone who has drunk far too much.

clue.text: A wet roof is dodgy – something you slip on?

indicators.note: dodgy means unsound or unreliable, so these letters cannot be trusted to stay in place

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rain-soaked roof is treacherous, the kind of surface you might slip on.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: you slip on shoes, not on a wet roof.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoes and slippers are slipped on to the feet, so the definition describes clothing for feet.

clue.text: Commotion in rugby, our side chasing Cork’s wingers

indicators.note: wingers play on the outside of a team, so only the outer letters are kept
to chase is to run after, so the piece named first comes later in the line

blocks.note: RU is the abbreviation for Rugby Union
the outer letters of the word
us is our side, as opposed to them

explanation.surface: A brawl breaks out at a rugby match as our team chases Cork's wing players.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chasing' puts our side after the Cork letters. Cork is an Irish county and its rugby team, which fits the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruckus is a noisy disturbance or row, a colloquial word for a commotion.

clue.text: Spell with Newcastle United ultimately pleased

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letters are kept

blocks.note: a charm is a magic spell
the last letter of the word
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A fan is delighted that Newcastle United finally had a good spell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newcastle United' reads as the football club, but each word gives only its last letter. 'Spell' is magic, not a period of play.
explanation.definitionFit: To be charmed is to be delighted, as in 'charmed to meet you', a stronger way of saying pleased.

clue.text: Cave in wood visited by everyone around

indicators.note: brought around means turned to face the other way, so the letters run backwards
a place visited by someone has that guest inside it

blocks.note: a copse is a small wood
all means everyone

explanation.surface: There is a cave in a wood that everyone round about visits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cave' reads as a noun, a hollow in the hillside, but 'Cave in' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To collapse is to fall in on itself, as a roof or tunnel does when it caves in.

clue.text: Map’s dot represented German city

indicators.note: something represented is presented anew in another form, so these letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dot on a map stands for a city in Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Represented' reads as a map symbol standing for a place, but it signals rearranging the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Potsdam is the capital of Brandenburg, near Berlin, an example of a city in Germany.

clue.text: Waiting for Godot demanding for the audience? Act withdrawn

definitions.text: Waiting for Godot demanding for the audience

blocks.clueFragment: Waiting for Godot demanding for the audience
blocks.note: first meaning, read cryptically: Beckett's drama is a play that spectators find difficult to understand, or get
second meaning: to behave aloof, feigning lack of interest

explanation.surface: A theatre critic calls Beckett's absurdist drama heavy going for spectators.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a cryptic reading: Waiting for Godot is a famously baffling play, hard for an audience to get, meaning to understand.
explanation.definitionFit: To play hard to get is to feign indifference or aloofness when being courted, which is acting withdrawn.

clue.text: Cheats almost rose to accept fine

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
to accept is to take in, so one piece is received inside another

blocks.note: the flower, with its last letter dropped
OK means fine

explanation.surface: Cheaters nearly stood up to accept a fine as punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like the past tense of rise, but it is the flower; 'fine' is OK, not a penalty.
explanation.definitionFit: To rook someone is to swindle them, so the verb rooks means defrauds, in the same tense as the definition.

clue.text: Close to rearing horse in protest

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: the last letter of the word
a roan is a horse with a mixed-colour coat

explanation.surface: A horse rears up in protest when someone comes near.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' reads as near, but it means the end of the next word; 'rearing' looks like a reversal signal and is not one.
explanation.definitionFit: A groan is a deep sound of complaint or disapproval, which works as a noun for a protest.

clue.text: Textile worker lifting tip of yarn dipped in colour?

indicators.note: the tip of something is its very end, here its first letter
lifting raises something up, and in a down entry that turns the letters upside down
a thing dipped in liquid goes inside it, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
red is a colour

explanation.surface: A worker in a textile mill dips the end of the yarn into dye.
explanation.walkthrough: Reverse the colour in this down clue, then dip the yarn's first letter into it.
explanation.definitionFit: A dyer colours fabric and thread for a living, one of the trades in the cloth industry.

clue.text: Distinctive feature, one on Mars possibly

indicators.note: possibly means in some possible form, so these letters may take another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A notable landmark is found on the planet Mars.
explanation.walkthrough: Mars suggests the planet or the Roman god, which fits the answer nicely, but it is only anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman nose has a prominent bridge, so it is a striking facial characteristic that marks out a face.

clue.text: Ordinary day ending in feud exhausted Lucy, weirdly

indicators.note: an ending is the last part, so only the final letter is kept
exhausted means emptied out, so the inside goes and only the outer letters stay

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for ordinary, as in O level
D is the abbreviation for day
the last letter of the word
the outer letters of the name

explanation.surface: An everyday quarrel ends with Lucy strangely worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: O level was the old ordinary-level British school exam, hence O for ordinary.
explanation.definitionFit: Oddly and weirdly are synonymous adverbs, both meaning in a strange or peculiar manner.

clue.text: Bird going back in rhododendrons

indicators.note: in means inside, so the letters sit within the following word
going back means travelling the opposite way, so read the letters right to left

blocks.note: the letters sit inside the shrub's name

explanation.surface: A bird retreats into the rhododendron bushes.
explanation.walkthrough: The run of letters can be read forwards in the shrub's name too, but 'going back' asks for it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The dodo was a flightless species from Mauritius, hunted to extinction, an example of the class named.

clue.text: A mostly great honour Queen gives Patrick Moore, perhaps

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: taken as written
strong in the sense of great, with its last letter dropped
OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: The Queen bestows a great honour on Patrick Moore.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits: Moore was knighted. Sir Patrick Moore presented the BBC stargazing programme The Sky at Night for over fifty years.
explanation.definitionFit: Patrick Moore was a famous British stargazer, an example of a scientist who studies stars and planets.
